Unfortunately, our result only establishes a guarantee for one execution of the protocol among n parties. It is worth emphasizing at the outset that the adversary is static and semi-honest, and that it corrupts at most t parties, where t < n/2. This is admittedly a restricted setting, and it is important not to lose sight of these restrictions. Furthermore, the setup-facing resource layer consists of ideal preprocessing from F_corr, so our result should not be read as providing a concrete implementation of F_corr.

Turning now to the simulation-facing machinery, the simulator receives the corrupted parties' inputs and outputs. This arrangement facilitates a comparison of the real and simulated joint views. More specifically, the statistical distance between these two joint views is at most 2^(-kappa). This bound is the bound on the joint views in the setting just described. We should stress again that the claim concerns one execution and does not establish security for malicious adversaries or adaptive corruption.

From the perspective of the online communication layer, the protocol uses two broadcast rounds in the online phase. Although this is the online round count, it is not a count that includes preprocessing. We must acknowledge this exclusion when discussing the two-round online phase. Finally, we should reiterate that the result does not cover reuse of preprocessing, and that a concrete implementation of F_corr is outside the claim made here.
